dossier.public_summary: A 3.6 Earth-radius flat-bottomed dip repeats every 7.03 days with no odd-even difference and a steady depth, on a cool small star with no nearby star that could mimic it. A modest brightness swing tracks the star's own 12170 ppm spot signal, not a second stellar eclipse. The size and flat shape together make a planet the best explanation, with follow-up needed to confirm activity and rule out the weak secondary signal.

reasons.why: Strongly flat-bottomed (negative V significance) favours a planet transit over a V-shaped grazing EB. Duration ratio 1.533 and fit_b 0.1011 are consistent with a central, flat dip.
Sub-Neptune size well below the 10-22 Re giant/star boundary, with rp_over_rstar 0.1067, positively planet-sized even with dilution correction.
Only one sector (91) with 3 transits gives a steady depth (chi2 0, dof 0) and no depth variability; transit_depths share 0.4285 spread across events, inconsistent with a few bad transits noise.
No plausible neighbour inside a TESS pixel can cause the 11370 ppm dip even with 25% eclipse, with closest that can at 42.5 arcsec needing 0.3599 eclipse. No off-target evidence.

Modest swing and marginal secondary at phase 0.5852 (not 0.5) just below significant detection threshold, consistent with stellar variability on an active M dwarf (rotation amplitude 12170 ppm) rather than a stellar EB; odd_even diff_sigma 1.936 shows no odd/even difference.
